reference.source: ATS/ERS alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency guidance and respiratory texts
clinicalPearls: Suspect in emphysema presenting at a young age, in a never-smoker or light smoker, or with a strong family history
The emphysema is classically panacinar and basal (lower-zone) predominant, in contrast to the upper-zone centrilobular pattern of typical smoking-related disease
The severe deficiency genotype is most often PiZZ, and testing includes serum alpha-1-antitrypsin level with phenotyping or genotyping
Smoking dramatically accelerates lung destruction, so smoking cessation is the single most important intervention
Coexisting liver disease can occur because the abnormal Z protein polymerises and is retained within hepatocytes
Intravenous augmentation therapy with pooled human alpha-1-antitrypsin is the specific disease-directed treatment for emphysema in suitable deficient patients
All patients with COPD should be tested at least once, as recommended by guidelines, since the condition is under-recognised
reference.pathophysiology: Alpha-1-antitrypsin is a protease inhibitor made in the liver that protects the lung from neutrophil elastase. In the common Z variant of SERPINA1, the abnormal protein misfolds and polymerises within hepatocytes, so little is secreted into the circulation. The resulting deficiency leaves the lung interstitium unprotected against elastase, particularly when neutrophil recruitment is amplified by cigarette smoke, leading to progressive destruction of alveolar walls and panacinar emphysema. Hepatic retention of the polymerised protein separately drives liver injury.
additionalDifferentials: Usual smoking-related chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Other causes of basal lung disease
Congenital lobar or bullous lung disease
additionalInvestigations: Pulmonary function tests demonstrating airflow obstruction and reduced gas transfer
High-resolution chest computed tomography showing basal panacinar emphysema
Liver function tests and hepatic assessment for associated liver disease
Family screening and genetic counselling for relatives
redFlags: Rapidly declining lung function or frequent exacerbations
Signs of chronic liver disease such as jaundice, ascites, or deranged synthetic function
Continued smoking in a confirmed deficient patient
Severe breathlessness or hypoxaemia indicating advanced emphysema
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends heavily on smoking status and baseline lung function; non-smokers may have near-normal life expectancy, whereas smokers with severe deficiency can develop disabling emphysema early, and augmentation therapy may slow the rate of lung tissue loss in selected patients.
pitfalls: Not testing for the deficiency in every patient diagnosed with COPD
Attributing early or basal emphysema solely to smoking
Failing to offer family screening once an index case is identified
references: ATS/ERS statement on the diagnosis and management of alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency
management: Smoking cessation is the most important intervention, dramatically slowing lung tissue loss; avoid environmental and occupational inhaled oxidants
Offer intravenous augmentation therapy with pooled human alpha-1-antitrypsin as the specific therapy for selected deficient patients with emphysema
Treat airflow obstruction with inhaled bronchodilators and corticosteroids, pulmonary rehabilitation and supplemental oxygen when hypoxaemic
Vaccinate against respiratory pathogens and treat infective exacerbations promptly
Monitor pulmonary function and screen for associated liver disease with hepatology input
Consider lung transplantation in end-stage emphysema
Provide family screening and genetic counselling for relatives
